name: Harassment (obscene initiated communication)
conduct: Initiating communication and, during it, making a comment, request, suggestion or proposal meeting §42.07(b)(3)’s specific obscene definition. Mere rude language is not automatically a patently offensive sexual-act/excretory description or solicitation. The actor must have intent to harass, annoy, alarm, abuse, torment or embarrass another, and the particular listed act must also be proved. Unwanted or upsetting expression is not automatically criminal. Constitutionally protected communications remain outside permissible punishment; application depends on the actual facts, not merely a listener’s displeasure. This ordinary branch excludes §42.07(c)’s special repeat, child-harm-intent, injunction, utility, court-employee and judge circumstances. Those circumstances can produce Class A, state jail or third-degree punishment and require their own findings.  This describes the retained current text, including amendments effective September 1 and December 4, 2025; conduct before those dates requires the applicable earlier version, not automatic use of the current grade.
penalty: Class B misdemeanor: ordinarily up to 180 days in jail, a fine up to $2,000, or both. Qualifying priors and other statutory findings can change the punishment; no repeat predicate is assumed.

name: Stalking (threat course)
conduct: On more than one occasion under the same scheme/course directed at a specific other person, knowingly engaging in the specified conduct. In addition to the underlying conduct, it must actually cause the specified fear of injury, death or an offense, or the listed harassed/terrified/intimidated/annoyed/alarmed/abused/tormented/embarrassed/offended reaction in the person or a listed family, household or dating partner, and would cause the corresponding statutory effect in a reasonable person in similar circumstances. Neither a single occasion nor only an objective reaction satisfies all three statutory parts. Different types of conduct may form the same course. The actor knows or reasonably should know the other person will regard the conduct as threatening injury/death to that person or an offense against the listed family/household/dating partner or property. For liability based on a true threat, constitutional protection requires at least recklessness about the communication’s threatening character; an objective reasonable-person finding alone does not resolve that requirement.  This ordinary profile does not assume a qualifying stalking prior.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Qualifying priors and other statutory findings can change the punishment; no repeat predicate is assumed.

name: Online impersonation (another person’s name/persona for web page)
conduct: Without the other person’s consent and with intent to harm, defraud, intimidate or threaten anyone, using that person’s name/persona to create a page on a commercial social-networking site or other Internet website. Mere resemblance or a name reference is not enough. Section 33.07(e) provides a defense for the listed service entities or conduct consisting solely of action as their employee. The exact entity and solely-employee conditions matter; an ordinary user does not automatically qualify. Qualification as a federally defined interactive computer service requires that separate incorporated definition, not a label supplied by this choice. Subsection (d) permits prosecution under this or another applicable law, but does not itself decide cumulative punishment.
penalty: Third-degree felony: ordinarily two to ten years in prison and a possible fine up to $10,000. Qualifying priors and other statutory findings can change the punishment; no repeat predicate is assumed.
